title: Burning pain in the ball of the foot or numb toes: is it Morton's neuroma?
seoTitle: Morton's Neuroma: Burning Ball-of-Foot Pain, Numb Toes
metaDescription: Burning ball-of-foot pain or a 'pebble in the shoe' feeling? What Morton's neuroma is, look-alikes to rule out, and treatment from shoes to surgery.
intro: Many people describe it the same way: it feels like a small stone is stuck under the front of the foot, and taking the shoe off and rubbing the toes brings relief. Often this is Morton's neuroma, an irritated nerve between the toes. It is uncomfortable, but it is not dangerous, and most people start with simple changes to footwear rather than an operation. A few look-alike problems do need ruling out, especially if you have diabetes.
summary: Morton's neuroma is a thickened, irritated nerve in the ball of the foot, usually between the third and fourth toes. It causes burning pain, tingling or numb toes and a 'pebble in the shoe' feeling. Wider, low-heeled shoes and a metatarsal pad are the first step; injections and surgery are kept for symptoms that persist.

sections.heading: What exactly is Morton's neuroma?
sections.body: Morton's neuroma is thickening and irritation of one of the small nerves that run between the toe bones to the toes. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), it usually forms between the third and fourth toes, and less often between the second and third. Despite the name, it is not a tumour and is not cancer. The nerve is squeezed between the bones of the forefoot, and with repeated pressure it becomes swollen and sensitive.

sections.heading: What does it feel like?
sections.body: The typical complaint is burning or sharp pain in the ball of the foot that can shoot into two neighbouring toes, along with a feeling of standing on a pebble or a fold in the sock. The NHS also lists tingling or numbness, and pain that gets worse in tight or high-heeled shoes. Symptoms are usually worse when walking and ease when the shoe comes off.
bullets: Burning, stabbing or sharp pain under the ball of the foot
A 'pebble' or 'marble' feeling under the forefoot
Tingling or numbness in two neighbouring toes
Relief from taking the shoe off and massaging the foot

sections.heading: Why does it happen?
sections.body: The exact cause is not fully known, but AAOS explains that pressure on the nerve plays a central part, and that high heels and tight, narrow shoes make it worse by squeezing the toe bones and pinching the nerve. The NHS adds a lot of running or other activities that put pressure on the feet, and foot shapes such as flat feet, high arches, bunions or hammer toes. Pointed office shoes and long hours of standing are common everyday triggers.

sections.heading: Could it be something else?
sections.body: Yes. Pain in the ball of the foot has several causes, and some matter more than a neuroma. General forefoot pain (metatarsalgia) and a stress fracture of a foot bone can feel similar; AAOS notes that X-rays are used to rule out a stress fracture or arthritis. In people with diabetes, numb or burning toes are more often due to nerve damage from diabetes itself, which needs a proper check rather than self-treatment.

table.caption: Common look-alikes for ball-of-foot pain
rows: Burning pain between two toes, 'pebble' feeling, better with shoes off
Wider shoes and a metatarsal pad; see a doctor if it persists
Aching under the ball of the foot, often under several toes
Cushioned footwear and activity change; get it assessed if not settling
Pain and swelling on top of the foot after a rise in walking, running or standing
Rest the foot and get examined; an X-ray may be needed
Numbness or burning in both feet, often all the toes
Get checked promptly and check your feet daily for sores

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.body: Diagnosis is mostly clinical: your doctor listens to how the pain behaves and presses between the toe bones to see whether it reproduces your symptoms, sometimes feeling a 'click' (Mulder's click). AAOS describes ultrasound as the preferred imaging test when a scan is needed, says MRI is usually not needed, and uses X-rays mainly to exclude a fracture or arthritis. Not everyone needs a scan.

sections.heading: What treatment works, and when is surgery considered?
sections.body: Most people start with footwear changes, and AAOS reports that this kind of non-surgical care gives relief in up to about 50% of patients. If that is not enough, a steroid injection can help some people for a while, but the evidence is less certain than its popularity suggests. Surgery is kept for symptoms that continue despite these steps, and it involves a real trade-off.
bullets: Shoes: wide toe box, low heel, soft sole; avoid tight, pointed shoes and high heels.
Metatarsal pad or insole: a small pad placed just behind the ball of the foot to spread the bones and take pressure off the nerve.
Activity change: reduce running, jumping and long hours in tight shoes while it settles.

Steroid injection: AAOS reports short-term relief in about 50 to 70% of patients. However, a Cochrane review (6 studies, 373 people) found that adding steroid to a local anaesthetic injection may make little to no difference to pain or function at 3 to 12 months, based on low-certainty evidence. Side effects such as thinning of the fat pad or lightening of the skin colour can occur.

Surgery (neurectomy): removing the affected segment of nerve. AAOS says surgery is considered if symptoms do not improve within 3 to 6 months or keep returning, and lists permanent numbness and a painful 'stump neuroma' as risks.

faqs.q: Is Morton's neuroma a tumour or cancer?
faqs.a: No. Despite the name, it is a thickened, irritated nerve between the toe bones, not a growth or cancer.

faqs.q: Will changing my shoes really help?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Wide, low-heeled, soft-soled shoes take pressure off the nerve, and AAOS reports that non-surgical care like this gives relief in up to about 50% of patients.

faqs.q: Does a steroid injection cure it?
faqs.a: It can ease pain for a while in some people, but a Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that adding steroid to an anaesthetic injection may make little difference at 3 to 12 months. It is an option, not a guaranteed fix.

faqs.q: If I have an operation, will my toes be numb?
faqs.a: With neurectomy, where part of the nerve is removed, AAOS lists permanent numbness between the affected toes as a known risk. This trade-off is worth discussing before choosing surgery.

faqs.q: I have diabetes and my toes feel numb. Is it Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: It may not be. Numbness in diabetes is often due to nerve damage from diabetes itself, so get your feet checked promptly, especially if you notice any sore or wound.
